lesson.title: Where the Charge Goes When the Source Disappears
lesson.summary: Once a charged capacitor is disconnected from its source and discharges through a resistor, its voltage decays exponentially from its initial value toward zero, releasing its stored energy as heat at a rate set by the same RC time constant.
lesson.body:
Now run the process from RC charging in reverse. A capacitor has been charged to some initial voltage V0, an initial condition set by whatever happened before, and then the source is removed, leaving the capacitor connected only to a resistor. With no source left to sustain it, the capacitor becomes the source, pushing its stored charge back out through the resistor until its voltage falls to zero. This is RC discharging, and it is the mechanism behind everything from a photoflash capacitor releasing its energy to the reason a piece of equipment can still deliver a shock seconds after being unplugged.

Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law to this now-sourceless loop gives v_C(t) = V0*e^(-t/RC), and the current i(t) = -(V0/R)*e^(-t/RC), where the negative sign simply reflects that current now flows out of the capacitor rather than into it, the opposite direction from charging. At t = 0 the exponential equals 1, so v_C starts at V0 exactly as the initial condition requires, and as t grows, v_C decays smoothly toward zero without ever reaching it in finite time.

The same self-limiting logic that produced exponential charging produces exponential decay here. The discharge current is proportional to whatever voltage remains on the capacitor, i = v_C/R. When v_C is large, current is large and charge drains quickly. As v_C falls, less voltage is available to drive current through R, so the rate of loss slows down along with it. A quantity whose rate of decrease is proportional to its own remaining value always decays exponentially, which is exactly what happens here.

Suppose a capacitor has been charged to V0 = 12 V and is then discharged through R = 4.7 k ohms with C = 220 microfarads. The time constant is tau = R*C = 4700 ohms times 0.00022 farads, which is 1.034 seconds. After one time constant, v_C = 12*e^-1 = 12*0.3679 = 4.42 V. After two time constants, roughly 2.07 seconds, v_C = 12*e^-2 = 12*0.1353 = 1.62 V. If you needed to know how long until the voltage drops to a safe touch level of 1 V, solve 12*e^(-t/1.034) = 1, giving e^(-t/1.034) = 0.0833, so t/1.034 = -ln(0.0833) = 2.485, and t = 2.485*1.034 = 2.57 seconds.

All the energy that was stored on the capacitor eventually ends up as heat in the resistor, since discharging offers no other place for it to go. That initial stored energy was (1/2)*C*V0^2 = 0.5*0.00022 F*144 V^2 = 0.01584 J, or 15.84 mJ, and every bit of it is dissipated in R by the time the capacitor reaches zero. This is exactly why power supply designs often include a deliberate bleeder resistor across large filter capacitors: without one, a capacitor charged to a hazardous voltage can sit there for a long time after the power is switched off, and the discharge time calculation above is precisely how an engineer sizes that resistor to make the equipment safe within a specified number of seconds.
